questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following muscle divides the axillary artery into 3 parts?
questions.explanation: The axillary artery is divided into three parts by the pectoralis minor muscle. It is the continuation of the subclavian artery from the outer border of the first rib to the lower border of teres major, after which it becomes the brachial artery. questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 57-year-old man presents with pain, numbness, and fatigue of the right arm. Angiography reveals decreased flow through the vessels anastomosing near the surgical neck of the humerus. The pathology is likely to be present in which of the following arteries?
questions.explanation: Branches of the third part of the axillary artery supply the surgical-neck region of the humerus. The source names the anterior circumflex humeral, posterior circumflex humeral and subscapular arteries, noting that the subscapular artery is not involved in the local anastomosis. A surgical-neck fracture can injure the posterior circumflex humeral artery and accompanying axillary nerve; positional compression can also occur in throwing athletes.

questions.question: Angiography of the upper limb vessels in a patient shows a blockage in the brachial artery. All of the following vessels will have decreased flow, except:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: An intern was asked to collect a sample for arterial blood gas analysis. Before puncturing the artery, she performed a modified Allen's test to assess the circulation. However, the test result was negative. What is the inference?

options.text: Radial circulation is inadequate, hence, ulnar artery should be punctured
Radial circulation is inadequate, hence, ulnar artery should not be punctured
Ulnar circulation is inadequate, hence, radial artery should be punctured
Ulnar circulation is inadequate, hence, radial artery should not be punctured

questions.correctAnswerText: Ulnar circulation is inadequate, hence, radial artery should not be punctured
questions.explanation: A negative modified Allen's test implies inadequate ulnar collateral circulation, so the radial artery should not be punctured. The test is performed before radial-artery instrumentation to assess the integrity of the superficial/deep palmar arches and ulnar patency. The patient makes a tight fist while both radial and ulnar arteries are compressed, then the hand is opened and ulnar compression is released. Return of color including the thumb is a positive test; failure of the hand to flush within about 5-15 seconds is negative and indicates inadequate ulnar circulation.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with end-stage renal disease was planning to undergo hemodialysis. An arteriovenous fistula was created on his forearm. This procedure is done mainly to achieve a minimum venous flow rate of:
questions.explanation: Hemodialysis requires substantial flow; the source states approximately 250-500 mL/min. The source lists two examples: radial artery to cephalic vein at the wrist (most common) and brachial artery to cephalic vein at the elbow.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Palmar venous network in the palm of hand gives rise to which of the following veins?
questions.explanation: The palmar venous network gives rise to the median antebrachial vein. This is a superficial vein of the anterior forearm; it drains superficial structures of the forearm and wrist and ascends toward the cubital fossa, where it may divide into median cephalic and median basilic veins in an inverted Y configuration. The dorsal venous network gives rise to the cephalic and basilic veins.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: You are asked to send a blood sample for complete blood count analysis of a clinically anemic patient. Sampling from which of the following vein is preferred?
questions.explanation: The antecubital vein (median cubital vein) is the preferred vein for direct blood sampling. The source notes that it connects the cephalic and basilic veins at the roof of the cubital fossa, lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis and is readily accessible. It is also used for IV injections, blood transfusions and blood withdrawal. The source reviews the cephalic, basilic and brachial veins as alternatives/anatomical relations.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a pre-axial vein?
questions.explanation: The cephalic vein is a pre-axial vein. Pre-axial and post-axial borders are named according to their position relative to the limb axis. In the adult upper limb the radial/outer border is pre-axial and carries the cephalic vein, while the ulnar/inner border is post-axial and carries the basilic vein.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with breast carcinoma was planned for a mastectomy. During the procedure, a blue dye was injected to map the flow of lymphatic drainage in the axillary lymph nodes. Which of the following will receive lymphatic drainage from the rest of the axillary lymph node groups?
questions.explanation: The apical group receives lymphatic drainage from the remaining axillary lymph-node groups and is therefore also called the terminal axillary lymph-node group. The source summarizes drainage as anterior, posterior and lateral groups -> central group -> apical group, followed by drainage to supraclavicular nodes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding axillary lymph nodes is false?

options.text: Posterior group lies along subscapular vessels
Lateral group lies along lateral thoracic vessels
Apical group lies along axillary vessels
Axillary lymph nodes drains trunk above the umbilicus

questions.correctAnswerText: Lateral group lies along lateral thoracic vessels
questions.explanation: The false statement is that the lateral group lies along the lateral thoracic vessels. The source places the lateral/humeral group posteromedial to the axillary vein, while the anterior/pectoral group lies along the lateral thoracic vessels. Axillary lymph nodes collectively drain the entire upper limb, breast and trunk above the umbilicus. The source divides them into lateral/humeral, anterior/pectoral, posterior/subscapular, central and apical groups and tabulates their locations, afferents and efferents.
